text.p: The following are the main stories from Monday morning's German newspapers:
FRANKFURTER ALLGEMEINE ZEITUNG
- Demands from Bavaria's Christian Social Union for a cabinet reshuffle continue.
- Chancellor Helmut Kohl says he wants to push through at least part of government tax reform plans.
- Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel says introduction of European economic and monetary union must not be postponed.
- Germany will have lost world market share in 1997, German Chambers of Commerce and Industry (DIHT) predict.
- Protection group for small shareholders warns against panic in wake of Wall Street fall.
HANDELSBLATT
- Politicians from major parties demand tougher measures to force unemployed people to accept work.
- Parliamentary commission says future of Germany as an industrial location is uncertain unless the state slims down.
- BMW boss Bernd Pischetsrieder calls for change in balance between indirect and direct taxation.
SUEDDEUTSCHE ZEITUNG
- Chancellor Helmut Kohl pledges not to accept a soft single European currency.
- Health insurance funds fear big rise in cost of medicines next year.
- Kohl says Geman contributions to European Union are too high.
- Prices for petrol, diesel and heating oil are relatively inexpensive in Germany, compared to prices in other European countries.
DIE WELT
- Kohl stresses timetable and criteria for monetary union.
- Row over plans to reform pensions system intensifies between government and opposition.
- Holocaust victims and their relatives want 29 billion marks from European insurance companies.
